key: Hal Millersen woke to find his window furred
prev: On the first morning of November, the world went white and crunchy, like a cookie somebody had sat on.
text: Hal Millersen woke to find his window furred over with feathers of ice. He scraped a hole in it with his thumbnail and looked out. The mill yard glittered. The stream, which had hummed so loudly in the autumn and slept so peacefully since, wore a thin crust of ice along its edges, like the rim of a pie. His breath made a small cloud, and he blew it at the glass to see how far it would go.

text: Downstairs the kitchen smelled of porridge and woodsmoke and, for the fourth morning in a row, pickled onions. Hal’s mother sat at the table with a bowl of them in front of her and a look of deep contentment. She had been tired since the harvest. She had fallen asleep twice in the bread basket. She had asked for pickled onions at breakfast, and nobody had understood it, and Hal’s father, who had a limp now instead of a crutch, had stopped saying anything in the way a sensible man does.

text: The cart stopped in the yard. The woman jumped down, quite lightly, and looked round at the mill, the wheel, the stream, the frost, and the boy with the slate.

prev: “I see,” said Dr. Liang. “Then I shall treat him with respect.” She glanced at the skeleton. “That is not a person. That is for teaching. I am afraid it is a very good listener, and it does not say much either.”
text: The boy, Wen, had not said anything. He had climbed down, set his toolbox on the ground, and was looking up at the gable end of the mill. High under the roof, over the loading door, there was a clock. It had a white face and black hands, and it had said ten past four since long before Hal was born. Wen looked at it the way you look at a tooth that hurts.

text: It took a long time. A bit of old oil dripped down, and then a spring, and then a very small cog that went rolling across the yard and was fetched by Gucci. At the top Wen did something to the back of the clock with a slow, careful, patient look, as if he had all the time in the world and the clock knew it. The village came out to see. A baby cried somewhere. The miller leaned on his doorpost and said he would believe it when he heard it.

text: It was the first thing Wen had said. Hal, at the bottom of the ladder, felt a small warm glow, the kind you get when somebody says something exactly right.

Pip had turned seven in the summer and mentioned it to everybody. He was holding a crust in each hand and watching the tin with great concentration.

text: Everybody turned. Scally looked at him. He had never seen the boy before, and he did not care for the way he was looking at the tin.

text: Hopsi had unwrapped one of her scarves to look at the sign again. She walked up to the tin and looked into it for a moment. When she spoke, it was in the quiet, even, ordinary voice that always made Scally feel as though his collar had got smaller.

prev: “I know,” said Wen, shaking it gravely. “Your friend’s mother told me to count my fingers afterward.”
text: “I have not got a mother like that,” said Scally, and counted them anyway. They were all there. He seemed a little disappointed.

prev: Everyone listened. The wind moved in the bare hedge. A cart creaked. Nothing else.
text: But beside Hal, the great gray wolf had gone perfectly still. His ears were pricked, and every hair along his back stood up, and he was looking at the hill and not at anyone else at all.

key: He did not howl like a wolf in a story, with
prev: Gucci howled at the wall all night.
text: He did not howl like a wolf in a story, with his nose to the moon. He howled the way a very large dog complains to a very small door: a long, low, worried grumble, with sudden sharp yaps in it. Hal lay awake with a pillow over his head. Down in the village, a hundred windows lit up and went dark again.

prev: “Then let us ask the doctor,” said Tabitha. “Doctors know about ears.”
text: Dr. Liang’s house stood by the bridge, a small crooked house with a blue door and a brass plate that said DOCTOR in letters so new they squeaked. Smoke curled from the chimney. Somebody had already hung out the washing, and it hung in a long, stiff, frozen row across the garden: shirts like boards, a nightdress standing up on its own, and six socks held out sideways by the frost, like a line of little dancers.

key: Inside, the house smelled of soap and woodsmo
prev: “Come in,” said Wen. “She likes worried.”
text: Inside, the house smelled of soap and woodsmoke and something sharp and clean that made Hal’s nose tingle. There was a big wooden table in the middle, and on it lay a long white sheet, and on the sheet sat the black leather bag. It was open. Out of it came a tangle of things Hal had never seen: a shiny silver tube with a hollow disc at one end, a small hammer with a rubber head, a lamp the size of a pencil, and a row of bottles with corks in them, in every color, like candy in a store window.

key: Thump-thump. Thump-thump. Thump-thump. It was
prev: He had never heard it before.
text: Thump-thump. Thump-thump. Thump-thump. It was small, and busy, and very close, and it did not stop for a single second. It had been going all his life, without once being asked, and it had never needed winding.

key: Gucci had never in his life been asked to sta
prev: “Now the wolf,” said Dr. Liang.
text: Gucci had never in his life been asked to stand still for anything. He stood still. He let the cold disc go against his great gray side, with his eyes rolling toward Hal in case this was a trick, and Dr. Liang closed her own eyes and listened, and so did the five of them, in turn, with the ends in their ears. It was slow and enormous: BOOM… BOOM… BOOM… like somebody knocking, very patiently, at the other side of a hill.

prev: “I do not know either,” said Hopsi. It was the first thing she had said since the gate, and she said it in a very small, pleased voice, the way people say it when they have found somebody who will say it back.
text: While all this was going on, Pip had been good. He had been so good that nobody had noticed him at all.

prev: “Do not drink that,” said Dr. Liang, perfectly calmly, and in a voice that made the whole room stand up straight. She crossed the floor in two steps and took the bottle out of his hand, put the cork back, and set it up on the high shelf, out of reach of anyone shorter than a door.
text: “It was only going to be a little bit,” said Pip. His lip had begun to wobble. “It smells like strawberries.”

prev: “No,” said Pip.
text: “You never take any medicine, or any pill, or any pink bottle, unless a grown-up you know well gives it to you: your mother, your father, me. Not your friend. Not a bottle you found. Not a bottle that smells nice. Never.” She looked round at them all, at the children, and at the silent wolf. “That goes for all of you. A doctor’s bag is not a toy, and not a store, and not a game.”

text: It had been standing by the back door the whole time, a great, round, tin churn, as tall as Titch, with a wide mouth and a brass handle. It had come with the house. Nobody had noticed Pip go round to it. They noticed only when there was a muffled, hollow, echoing noise, like somebody shouting at the bottom of a well.

prev: “Stop,” said Wen.
text: He had been standing still. Now he put down his kettle, and came across the floor, and knelt beside the churn, and looked at the rim. It was a narrow neck, a little too small for the ears. “If you pull,” he said, “the ears catch. Pulling makes a head bigger. I mean, it makes it feel bigger, because the ears bend. We should make the neck slippery. Is there anything slippery?”

text: It took a whole pat of butter and a long, quiet minute. Wen spread it round the rim of the churn, with his tongue between his teeth. Titch and Tabitha held the churn. Hal, because it seemed right, held the top of Pip’s pants. “Now,” said Wen, and Pip tipped his head, and one red ear went through the neck, and then the other, and then, all at once, with a noise like a cork leaving a bottle, the whole of Pip came out, backwards, in a shower of buttery milk, and sat down on the floor with his hair in spikes.

text: When they had cleaned up the kitchen, and washed Pip, and given him a bun, the five of them found that they were all standing in a ring round Wen, who had not been given anything.

prev: Hal gave him a stick of chalk. Titch gave him a crust, with a great deal of ceremony, torn in an even half, and Tabitha gave him an apple, because she always had one. Pip, who was still damp, offered him a very good stone. Gucci offered a bone, which was accepted, though not with enthusiasm.
text: Scally had been standing a little apart, with his hands behind his back. He had been working on something, and it had not been going well. It had been going to be a watch. It was a button, and he had been going to say that it was a watch. He had thought of the candy on the shelf. He had thought of a very small lie, a perfectly good small lie, about a gold ring he did not have.

text: “Thank you,” he said. “It is the best one. I have never been given a sock.” He turned the hops over in his other pocket, and the chalk, and the crust, and the apple, and the stone, and the bone, and looked as if he did not know what to do with his face. “I do not think I know how to say this properly. Nobody has given me so many things at once.”

text: By the end of the week the mill pond had frozen over, and the whole village went down to look at it.

text: He was kneeling on the bank, at the very edge. He had his screwdriver in one hand and a knitting needle from Dr. Liang’s kitchen in the other, and he was pushing the needle slowly down through a crack in the white ice at the edge, until it stopped. Then he pulled it out, and held it up, and measured it against his thumb.

text: “It is the weak kind,” said Wen, without looking up. “White ice is full of little bubbles and snow. It is about half as strong. Clear ice is the strong kind. It looks like black glass.”

text: Scally opened his mouth, and found that there was a boy at the end of it who had counted everything since the day he arrived. He shut his mouth. “It is a small pond,” he said. “Small tracks.”

text: Pip said it, too. He said it with his best face, the face he wore when he was being good. Then he went and stood at the edge of the pond, a little apart from the others, with his hands in his pockets, whistling the way he did when he was thinking about something.

text: He did not run. He walked, carefully, with his arms out, like a person on a log, along a line of clear gray ice. He was ten steps out. He was twenty. He turned, and waved, and shouted, “I can walk on water!” in a very happy voice, and the whole bank of grown-ups and children and cocoa went silent at the same time.

text: The whole bank was moving at once. Hal’s mother had dropped the cocoa. Gucci ran up and down the edge, whining, and was caught by the collar by Tabitha. Scally had gone the color of porridge, and the sign had fallen out of his hand.

key: “Throw it low,” said Wen. “So it slides. Not

text: “Throw it low,” said Wen. “So it slides. Not up in the air. It has to land beside him, and he has to be able to grab it without moving his feet.”

text: Pip lay down on the ice. He did it so slowly that it took a century. The ice groaned again, and one tiny piece of it near his hand flicked loose and slid away. He lay there, flat, with his red cap on the glass and his nose an inch from the gray ice, and his legs stuck out behind him.

key: They all pulled. Hal and Tabitha and Titch, w
prev: “Pull!” said Titch.
text: They all pulled. Hal and Tabitha and Titch, with Hal’s mother behind them gripping the end of the rope and Gucci tugging at the loop by his teeth, and Pip slid across the ice on his belly, like a very small sled, with his arms stretched out in front of him. Behind him, as he left, the ice cracked, and cracked again, and then at the spot where he had been standing, with a sound like somebody tearing a sheet, the whole piece of the pond sank, and a round black hole opened up, and the dark water slopped up over the edge.

key: “I did not test it,” said Scally. He said it

text: “I did not test it,” said Scally. He said it louder. He turned round and said it to everybody, to the whole bank of faces. “I did not go out there. I did not test it at all. I just wanted the nickels. I said it was perfect because if I said it was perfect, you would pay.” His voice shook. “And Pip heard me. And he believed me.”

text: For a moment nobody moved. Then Hal’s mother made a very odd noise, and Titch lifted her face from her knees and began to laugh, with the tears still running down it, and then everybody was laughing, the shaky laughing of people who have been very frightened and have found out it was all right. Scally pulled off a boot. He pulled off a sock, and held it out, and Pip took it and put it on his hand like a mitten.

text: Dr. Liang looked at her son. She did not say anything. She put her hand on his head, very lightly, for a moment, the way you might put your hand on a clock that you loved.

text: The ice melted, and froze again, and melted again, and in the third week of December the hill began to click in earnest.

text: “I did. All eleven. And the church tower, from the outside.” He frowned. “It is not coming from a clock.”

text: “Just a little, just a bit,” said a small voice at the bottom of the steps. It was Pip, with a crust in each fist, sitting on the bottom step with his chin on his knees. text: First, Hal asked his mother. She was at the kitchen table, with a bowl of pickled onions and a very large knitting project that she had not yet explained, and she looked at him over the top of the needles for a long moment. “Where?” she said.

text: “I am not,” said Wen, “a person who likes the dark.” He said it all in one breath, in a rather flat, dry voice. He was holding the lantern in both hands, and his knuckles were white. “I thought I should mention it, in case I do something strange.”

text: The passage opened out suddenly into a chamber, about the size of the mill kitchen, with a roof so high that the lantern light did not reach the top. The floor was wet and sandy. And all across the ceiling, and down the walls in long uneven rows, hung small brown bundles, hundreds and hundreds of them, close together, quite still.

prev: “Bats,” said Tabitha.
text: She had said it softly, with her face tipped up and her eyes very wide. “My gran has them in the sea caves, by her house. She calls them the sleepers. They hang by their toes. She says if you are quiet in winter they will stay asleep, and if you wake them, they have to burn their food to stay warm, and then they run out before spring.”

text: He took it out, slowly. It was not easy for him. He put the cold silver disc to the air, a foot from the nearest sleeper, not touching it at all, and held his breath. “I cannot hear it,” he said. “It is too far. It is too small.”

text: It did it slowly. A small black wing opened, thin as a leaf, and a tiny face turned, with a nose like a crumpled button, and two enormous ears that went round, and round, listening. It opened its mouth. It made no sound that any of them could hear. But Wen, who was holding the lantern, felt the whole air hum, very faintly, against his face, and from somewhere up in the dark came the little, quick, dry noise he had heard every night for a month.

text: It was just past two in the afternoon. They were on their way down the hill, tired and quiet and very pleased, when Titch, who was walking ahead, stopped in the path.

prev: The trouble with a rumor is that it runs faster than the people who start it.
text: By the next morning the whole village knew about the bats. Nobody knew exactly what they knew, which is the usual way with a rumor. Mrs. Crumb had heard that there were a thousand of them. The butcher had heard there were ten thousand, and that they were the size of dogs. Somebody’s uncle, who had once seen a bat in a barn in another valley, had heard they got tangled in your hair and could not be got out.

text: It was the first thing Hopsi had said all morning. “It was a very good idea,” she said, in a low voice, “for a person who knows that bats do not get in your hair.”

prev: Everybody turned. A good many of them were wearing brown paper hats.
text: “As you know,” said the Mayor, “this village has many fine things. We have a mill. We have a bridge. We have the finest bread for twenty miles. And what we have not got,” and here he flung out one arm, “is a proper cheese cellar!”

key: “Ah,” said the Mayor. “Yes. The bats.” He low
prev: “What about the bats?” called somebody.
text: “Ah,” said the Mayor. “Yes. The bats.” He lowered his voice, and every person in the crowd leaned forward. “I am told they are filthy. I am told they carry disease. I am told they fly into your hair, and bite, and make a nest. It is high time somebody did something. And I,” he said, thumping his chest, “am that somebody.”

prev: “Then somebody should find out. Before the rock goes over the door.” He looked at the Mayor, standing on his barrel, and then at the paper hats, and then, slowly and thoughtfully, at the boy who sold them. “And somebody,” he added, “who knows a lot about hats.”
text: Scally was standing still. All the color had gone out of his face. His hand was on the edge of the table, and the paper hats beneath it had begun to tremble, very slightly, from the shaking of the table.

text: For a long moment, Scally did not move. Then he took a very deep breath, climbed up onto the baker’s step with the sign in his hand, and said, in a voice that carried over the whole crowd, “Excuse me!”

text: “They do not,” said Scally. “I made it up. I made it up so I could sell you a hat. They are the size of a thumb. They hang upside down and sleep. They are in the cave right now, hundreds of them, and I saw them, and they are not filthy, and they are not dangerous. They are only asleep, and cold, and small, and if you put a rock over the door, they will not get to wake up.” His voice shook. “I am sorry. Your hats are free. I will give you all your money back. I will give you all your nickels.”

text: “The boy is right,” said Dr. Liang. “I am a doctor, and I will tell you what I know, and I will tell you what I do not. Bats do not get tangled in hair. They are very good at flying, and they can see and hear perfectly well. A few bats, in the whole world, carry a disease called rabies, and that is why you must never, ever touch one. Never pick one up, not even a sleeping one, not even a hurt one. If one is on the ground, you tell a grown-up and you stay away. But a bat that is left alone will not hurt you.

key: It was the third night after the village meet

text: It was the third night after the village meeting, and the five of them, with Hopsi and Gucci, were sitting on the floor of Dr. Liang’s back room, among a heap of bits and pieces that Wen had been collecting all week. There was a funnel from Mrs. Crumb’s kitchen. There was a long brass spring from the broken clock in the church tower. There was a small silver bell, four copper wires, a cork, three buttons, an old pocket watch with no hands, and a tin whistle that Scally had won off a peddler.

key: “Sound has a pitch,” said Wen. “High or low.
prev: “Too high?” said Pip.
text: “Sound has a pitch,” said Wen. “High or low. A tuba is low. A whistle is high. A mouse squeak is higher. And above that, there are sounds so high that human ears cannot catch them at all. My mother calls that ultrasound. Dogs can hear some of it. That is why Gucci howls.” He tapped his own ear. “Bats talk in it. They make a squeak, much too high for us, and they listen for it to come back.”

key: It was the strangest thing Hal had ever seen.
prev: He held it out, rather shyly, and they all looked at it.
text: It was the strangest thing Hal had ever seen. The funnel had been fixed to a bent length of copper pipe, with the brass spring wound round it and the bell hung from the narrow end. The pocket watch was strapped to one side, its ticking face turned inward. There were three buttons along the top, and a small cork stopper sat at the very end. It looked like a trumpet that had been taken apart and put back together by somebody who had only heard of trumpets from a friend.

prev: Everybody looked at Hopsi, who had gone quiet and thoughtful, the way she did when something was not quite right.
text: “I should say,” said Hopsi, slowly, “that I do not think it can work the way you say. A bat’s squeak is very high, and a spring cannot slow it down. A real machine for hearing bats uses electricity. It listens with a small wire, and turns the high sound into a lower one, with a kind of box.” She looked at the listener, and at Wen’s face, and made up her mind. “But this is a story. And at dusk, with the sun going down red behind the hill, and the first stars coming out, seven children and a wolf crept up the long slope to Hanger Hill,
text: They stopped a good way from the cave mouth. Dr. Liang had said that was the rule: quiet, and far enough away to give the sleepers room, and no lights shone at the cave. They crouched in the bracken. They waited. Pip fell asleep for a few minutes on Scally’s shoulder, and woke up, and said he had not.

key: He held out the funnel, and all of them liste
prev: “That is it,” said Wen, in an awed voice. “That is a bat. Listen.”
text: He held out the funnel, and all of them listened, one by one, with their heads close together. And they heard it: a small, dry, quick, rapid ticking, that sped up, and slowed, and sped up again, and finally rushed together into a long, soft, running buzz.

key: Over the hill, against the last green light,
prev: “It has found a moth,” said Dr. Liang quietly, from behind them. “That is called the feeding buzz. The squeaks come faster and faster as the bat gets closer. Each one is shorter than the last, so it can tell, almost to the inch, where the moth is, until it catches it.” She was smiling, in the dark. “That is
text: Over the hill, against the last green light, a small dark shape flickered out of the cave mouth, circled, once, twice, and was gone, as quick as a thought. Then another. Then another, a dozen, a hundred, in a whirling, fluttering river of tiny wings, pouring out of the hill and into the evening air, swooping and diving above the creek, over the bare hedges, round the church tower, and out across the fields to the village.

key: Scally, kneeling in the bracken with his arms
prev: “Then they cannot come out,” said Wen, “and they cannot go back. And there will be no bats. There will be no moths eaten. There will be no more of the quiet clicking.” His voice went very small. “There will be only cheese.”
text: Scally, kneeling in the bracken with his arms round his knees, had said nothing at all. His face was turned up to the sky. The last of the bats were wheeling high overhead, black as scraps of burnt paper, in front of a sky full of stars, and in their path a cloud of moths went whirling up and up.

key: It was a gray Saturday in the middle of Janua
prev: “Today,” said Dr. Liang, “we are going to see with sound.”
text: It was a gray Saturday in the middle of January, and the whole back room of the little blue-doored house had been cleared. The table stood against the wall. The skeleton in the hat had been moved to the corner, where he looked on, politely, with his empty eyes. In the middle of the floor stood a high narrow bed with a white sheet on it, and beside the bed, on a wheeled cart, stood a machine.

key: “It is a listening lantern,” said Dr. Liang.
prev: It was a sort of box, the size of a bread oven, made of brass and dark wood, with a small gray glass window set into the front, and a hand crank at one side. From the box ran a coiled cord to a smooth silver wand, about as big as a bar of soap. Nobody had ever seen anything
text: “It is a listening lantern,” said Dr. Liang. “It makes a sound too high for you to hear. It sends the sound in. The sound bounces off whatever it hits, and comes back, and the machine turns the echoes into a picture.” She smiled. “It is the same trick the bats use, and the same trick Hal used on the cliff. Sound goes out. Sound comes back. And from the time between, you can tell what is there.”

key: Titch’s mother had been sitting in the best c
prev: “Your mother’s,” said Dr. Liang. “If she is still willing.”
text: Titch’s mother had been sitting in the best chair with her hands folded on top of her round stomach, looking, for the first time that winter, a little nervous. She was a small, brisk, freckled woman, usually, with a voice that could be heard from the mill to the church. She said now, in a rather small voice, “I would like the children to see. It is a family thing.”

key: And from the box, very faintly, there came a
prev: “Wait,” said Dr. Liang. “Listen.”
text: And from the box, very faintly, there came a sound. It was fast and soft and fluttering, like a bird’s wing against a window, a quick, small, busy swish-swish-swish-swish. It went on and on.

key: Titch’s mother was crying a little, in an ext
prev: Nobody said anything at all.
text: Titch’s mother was crying a little, in an extremely happy way. Titch had gone very still, and then she reached out and took her mother’s hand, and held it hard. Wen had stopped turning the crank, and a very small light had come into his face, as though he had just seen the first clock that ever worked.

key: “I do not tell people what they are having,”
prev: “It is a he,” said Pip firmly. “I decided.”
text: “I do not tell people what they are having,” said Dr. Liang, in an amused voice, “unless they ask me. And I do not,” she added, “say anything about biscuits.”

key: They all had a turn at the window, to look at
prev: Nobody knew what he meant by that last line, and nobody asked.
text: They all had a turn at the window, to look at the picture. Gucci was allowed to put one huge paw on the edge of the cart, and sniff, and look stunned. Scally, who had been standing at the back with his hands in his pockets, said in a low voice that it was the best thing he had ever seen, even better than the bats. “That is a person,” he said. “In there. A person that nobody has met.”

key: Her voice was light and ordinary. But Hal, lo
prev: “Of course,” said Hal’s mother.
text: Her voice was light and ordinary. But Hal, looking up, saw that her face had gone quite pink, and her hand was resting flat on the front of her dress.

key: They went. The kitchen was warm and small and
prev: “Because I would like to talk to your mother about her dizzy spells,” said Dr. Liang gently. “And because I think she would rather you were not worried. Out you go.”
text: They went. The kitchen was warm and small and smelled of cocoa. Hal sat at the table with his slate in his hands, and said nothing, and listened to the sounds from the back room. There was the hand crank. There was a long, soft murmur of two voices. Then, through the wall, very distinctly, he heard his mother laugh. It was a short, astonished, helpless laugh, and then it stopped, and for a while, there was no sound at all, and then he heard a small noise, like someone drawing a long, shaky breath, and the sound of his mother saying, in a voice he did not know, “Oh.”

key: “Everything is perfectly fine,” she said. “I
prev: When the door opened, Hal’s mother came out with her eyes shining and her cheeks pink, and her hand on her middle. She walked straight over to the table and put her other hand on the top of Hal’s head, and stood there, quite still, looking down at him.
text: “Everything is perfectly fine,” she said. “I am healthy, and Dr. Liang says I am as strong as a horse. I will tell you all about it, my love. Soon. When I am ready. Is that all right?”

key: The big snow came the first week of February,
text: The big snow came the first week of February, and it came the way a very large dog comes into a room: all at once, and licking everything.

key: The long hill behind the mill was the best in
prev: There was no argument.
text: The long hill behind the mill was the best in the valley. It started up by the old oak, ran down a gentle slope, steepened in the middle, and finished in a long, sweet, flat run across the field, where a wall of hay bales had been stacked every winter for as long as anyone could remember. Beyond the bales was the village lane. Past the lane was the pond. Hal’s father had stood at the top of the hill that morning, with his cane, and said in a very firm voice that anybody who went past the bales would answer to him.

key: “Hmm,” said Dr. Liang, from her other side. S
prev: “I have had a funny little ache all morning,” said Titch’s mother. “It is nothing. It comes and goes. I am sure it is the cold.”
text: “Hmm,” said Dr. Liang, from her other side. She said nothing else. But she took out a small notebook, and wrote something in it, and put it back.

key: It was a long, low, handsome sled, made of pa
prev: Wen had built his.
text: It was a long, low, handsome sled, made of pale wood, with two runners as smooth as glass. On the front he had fitted a small brass bell. At the back, he had attached, by a hinge, a long wooden stick, and a rope that ran up to the handlebar.

key: It was the first time anyone had ever heard h
prev: “Race you,” said Wen.
text: It was the first time anyone had ever heard him say it. For a moment Scally was too astonished to answer. Then he put his boots on the baker’s big flat tray, which was his sled, and his eyes began to shine. He hummed, almost without noticing, under his breath: Just a little, just a bit—

key: They went again. Scally, on the baker’s tray,
prev: “Go again,” said Tabitha, calmly.
text: They went again. Scally, on the baker’s tray, with his hat over his eyes and his arms spread wide, went down the hill like a sailor on a ship in a storm, screaming with joy. Wen, on the Brass Bell, went smoothly and exactly in a long, quiet curve, steering with his heels, tinkling gently. Scally reached the bottom first. He kept going, straight over the bump, off the end of the tray, into the hay bale wall, and into the soft snow behind it, headfirst, with his legs sticking up. Wen arrived four seconds later, pulled the rope, and stopped one foot from the bales, with a small bell

key: “You are going to go over the little bump,” s
prev: “I am going to fly,” he said.
text: “You are going to go over the little bump,” said Titch, “and land in the soft part. And you are going to put your feet out in front of you, and not stand up, and not look back.”

key: The rest of the morning went by in a happy bl
prev: “You did,” said Titch. She sat down in the snow beside him, quite suddenly, and put her arm round him.
text: The rest of the morning went by in a happy blur. They built a fort, with walls as high as Hal’s chest, and a snowman beside it, which was meant to be tall and noble, and turned out short and lumpy, with a carrot nose that Gucci ate at once. They had a snowball fight, which Tabitha won, because she threw like a farmer. They were given hot chocolate, and a great many marshmallows, and Mrs. Crumb inspected all of them for frostbite, and found nothing.

key: “It is the best one so far,” said Hopsi. “I d
prev: Everybody looked at her.
text: “It is the best one so far,” said Hopsi. “I do not believe a word of it. It is true that he told it.” She gave one of her very small smiles. “I should not say that is a lie. That would not be fair.”

key: “Right now,” said Dr. Liang, and stood, and p
prev: “Already?” said Pip.
text: “Right now,” said Dr. Liang, and stood, and put a hand on Titch’s mother’s shoulder. Titch’s mother had gone quiet. She was holding the arms of her chair, quite tightly, and breathing out slowly through her mouth.

key: Hal always said that the first flake fell jus
prev: Nobody ever agreed afterward how quickly it came.
text: Hal always said that the first flake fell just as his father set Titch’s mother in the Crumb Express and tucked a quilt round her. Wen always said it was a few minutes later, when they were already halfway across the yard. Pip, who had been made to ride on the back with his washtub, said the sky fell in all at once, like a white blanket pulled off a bed. They all agreed on one thing: by the time Titch’s mother was settled in her own front room, with a fire lit and her feet on a stool, the world had gone.

key: She had come over from the hill at a run, wit
prev: “Right,” said Mrs. Crumb.
text: She had come over from the hill at a run, with her sleeves already rolled, and she stood in the middle of Titch’s front room, with her fists on her hips, like a general. She was a big, floury, comfortable woman, and she had been born in the village and had helped half of it into the world. “Nobody panic. Millie, you sit right there, and breathe like I showed you. Mr. Mitchel, you boil water. Mrs. Millersen, you are going to fetch every clean towel in this house, and you are going to sit down in between.” She turned. “Doctor, your bag?”

key: She went out into the white. The door shut. A
prev: “I will be back in fifteen minutes.” She put on her coat and wound her scarf round her face, and her eyes, above it, were very steady. “That is a promise. I keep them.”
text: She went out into the white. The door shut. And that was the last any of them saw of Dr. Liang for a very long time.

key: The men went out in a chain, tied together by
prev: “Yes, sir,” said everybody.
text: The men went out in a chain, tied together by the waist, to look for the doctor, and came back twenty minutes later, covered in white, shaking their heads. They could not find the bridge. They could not even find the lane. The wind had blown the snow into drifts as high as a man’s chest, and in the dark and the swirl, there was nothing to hold on to at all.

key: “A person who is lost in snow should stop,” s
prev: Nobody answered.
text: “A person who is lost in snow should stop,” said Wen. “She knows that. She told me so herself. Stop where you are, and stay still, and make a noise. But she has no whistle. She has no light. She cannot see the house. She cannot hear it.” He swallowed. “She cannot hear anything.”

key: It was the strangest scene any of them ever r
prev: They went to Hal’s father, who listened in silence, and looked at the white window, and said, “Show me.”
text: It was the strangest scene any of them ever remembered. They climbed to the dim loft above the mill, where the sacks were stacked, and the great wheel of the clock stood, with its gears and weights and pendulum, behind a little door in the gable. Hal’s father held the ladder. Hal held the lantern. Wen climbed up into the little dark space with a hammer and, with a face of terrible concentration, hit the great bell as hard as he could.

key: “She says it is where the wind was coming fro
prev: “Why west?” said Hal, from the foot of the ladder.
text: “She says it is where the wind was coming from. She says people walk into the wind without knowing.” He stopped for breath. “She says she thinks so. She does not know.”

key: “No,” said Hal’s father. “Not you. Not the ro
prev: “Gucci!” screamed Hal. He dived for the doorframe. Hal’s father caught him by the back of his sweater and held on.
text: “No,” said Hal’s father. “Not you. Not the rope. He is a wolf. He knows snow better than any of us. Let him go.”

key: It was a long ten minutes. Nobody spoke. Wen
prev: BONG.
text: It was a long ten minutes. Nobody spoke. Wen rang, and rang, with his arm aching and his lip bitten white, thirty seconds, thirty seconds, and the wind went on howling, and the great bell rolled out into the white night with a sound like the heart of the valley.

key: “I stopped,” said Dr. Liang. She was shaking
prev: He went down the ladder in about three rungs. He did not stop to take the lantern. The door of the mill was open, and out of the white, along the fence, hand over hand, with her coat covered in snow from collar to hem, and her scarf frozen stiff, and her black bag clutched in one hand, came Dr.
text: “I stopped,” said Dr. Liang. She was shaking all over, and she was laughing. “I did what I tell everybody to do. I found a fence, and I stood still, and I held on. And I heard a bell.” She looked up at the little dark window high in the gable. “I could not see anything. But I could hear the bell, and the bell said, this way, this way. And then the dog came out of the snow like a gray ghost, and took my sleeve in his teeth.”

key: Dr. Liang ran. She ran across the yard, along
prev: “In there,” said Hal.
text: Dr. Liang ran. She ran across the yard, along the rope, in her stiff, frozen coat, with the black bag swinging, and the door of the Mitchels’ house opened for her and closed again. And behind it, over the howling of the wind, over the slow, steady stroke of the bell, which Wen had just been told he could stop ringing, there rose a small, thin, furious sound that none of the children had ever heard before.

key: Mrs. Crumb came out of the little front room
prev: It was a boy.
text: Mrs. Crumb came out of the little front room at ten minutes past midnight, with a dish towel over one shoulder. She had one big hand on the door frame, and she was smiling so widely that her whole face seemed to be in danger. “A boy,” she said. “Seven pounds, near enough. Ten fingers, ten toes, and the loudest lungs in the valley. Mother and baby are fine. Fine, and tired. Nobody is to go in for five minutes.”

key: Pip had gone to sleep on the floor under the
prev: They had all gathered there, in the end, with the storm still howling at the windows. Hal’s father was there, with his cane across his knees, and Titch’s father, a large, quiet man with soot in the creases of his hands, who had boiled water for hours, and been told, and had sat down in a chair, put his face
text: Pip had gone to sleep on the floor under the table, with his washtub for a pillow. He woke up all at once at the noise, and sat up, and banged his head on the table, and said, “What?”

key: “I have got Pip, and Little Man, and Pipsquea
prev: “You have not got two.”
text: “I have got Pip, and Little Man, and Pipsqueak. That is three.” He put his shoulders back. “I am a big brother.”

key: Pip climbed up onto the bed. He put his elbow
prev: “Say hello,” said Titch’s mother, quietly.
text: Pip climbed up onto the bed. He put his elbows on the quilt and his chin on his hands, and looked, for a very long time, at the baby, a foot from his own face. The baby opened its eyes. They were dark, and cloudy, and unfocused, and wandered about the room, and finally came to rest, quite by accident, on Pip’s nose.

key: “Swish,” said Wen, in a whisper. “Swish-swish
prev: He put the cold silver disc against the front of the flannel, and held very still.
text: “Swish,” said Wen, in a whisper. “Swish-swish-swish-swish.” His eyes grew round. “It is the same. It is the same one. It is going just as fast as it did in the picture.”

key: Scally sat. He held out his arms, rigidly, th
prev: “Sit down on the end of the bed,” said Titch’s mother, “and hold out your arms.”
text: Scally sat. He held out his arms, rigidly, the way a person holds out a tray, and Titch’s mother laid the flannel bundle in them. For a long minute nobody breathed. The baby grunted, and squirmed, and settled, and opened his dark unfocused eyes and looked up at Scally’s face, and Scally, who had never in his life been quiet for more than eight seconds together, did not say a single word.

key: She had thought about it all evening, in the
prev: Hopsi was the last to give her present.
text: She had thought about it all evening, in the kitchen, in the quiet, while the others had been talking, and she had come to the conclusion that there was no true sentence in the world that was big enough. She could have said, “Welcome.” She could have said, “I hope you will be happy.” She could not say either of those, because she did not know. So she did what an elf does when the words are not allowed. She took something out of her sleeve, very quietly, and put it on the quilt, beside the baby’s tiny fist.

key: Outside the wind had begun to drop. The storm
prev: “It is the shortest true thing I know,” said Hopsi. “That is all.”
text: Outside the wind had begun to drop. The storm that had come like a giant dog was going away over the hills, slowly, with a sigh. In the east, over the long black ridge of Hanger Hill, the sky had begun to go gray, and then pink, and in the still, white, shining world a single clear star was shining low over the horizon.

key: It ran off the roofs in little silver waterfa
prev: The snow went home in April, all in one afternoon, like a guest who has suddenly remembered the time.
text: It ran off the roofs in little silver waterfalls. It slid off the mill wheel, which woke up with a groan and began, slowly, to turn. It left the fields in great brown patches, and the creek came down loud and brown and bubbling, carrying twigs, and there were snowdrops under the hedge, and a robin on the gatepost, and a smell in the air that was half mud and half something sweet, which was spring.

key: They had brought blankets. They had brought t
prev: There were forty people sitting on the hillside in the dusk, in neat rows on the damp grass, and nobody was talking.
text: They had brought blankets. They had brought thermoses, and sandwiches, and small children, and one very large wolf. In the middle of the front row, on a folded quilt, sat Hal and Wen and Titch and Tabitha, and Pip, who was holding the washtub, and Scally, and Hopsi in a single scarf for the first time that year. Titch was holding a small bundle. Behind them sat Dr. Liang with her black bag at her feet, and Hal’s father, and Mrs. Crumb, and the farmers, and the butcher, and a great many people who had said that they would come only for a minute.

key: Hal cleared his throat. “We went into the cav
prev: “Very well,” said the Mayor stiffly. He set down his wheel of cheese on the grass, and folded his arms. “Proceed.”
text: Hal cleared his throat. “We went into the cave in December,” he said, “with permission, and in daylight, and we did not touch anything. We looked. We counted. It took us three visits, because you cannot count four hundred bats at once.”

key: “The cabbage moth is the worst pest in this v
prev: A murmur went round the crowd.
text: “The cabbage moth is the worst pest in this valley,” said Hal, “and everybody knows it. Every year it eats a third of the cabbages, and it lays eggs in the granary, and in the flour. My father has lost whole sacks of grain to it, in the mill.” He looked at his father, who nodded, once. “The bats eat the moths. They do not eat the cabbages. They do not eat the flour. They do not charge a nickel.” He swallowed. “That is what we found out. And that is only what we can count.”

key: It came out low, and quick, and so small that
prev: Somebody gasped. A baby, in a blanket, said something that sounded like “Ba!” And then the first one came out of the cave.
text: It came out low, and quick, and so small that nobody was sure they had seen it. A little dark scrap, no bigger than a leaf, flittered up and round, in a loop, against the violet sky. Another followed. And another. Then, with a rush, like smoke from a chimney, like ink poured into water, like a long black ribbon unrolling from the rock, a hundred of them came pouring out of Hanger Hill together, whirling and twisting and flickering in the dusk, over the heads of the astonished crowd.

key: He stood in the grass, with his wheel of chee
prev: The Mayor had not moved.
text: He stood in the grass, with his wheel of cheese at his feet and his hat in his hand, looking up. He looked for a very long time. A bat came down, and passed so near his head that his mustache ruffled. He did not flinch. His mouth was a little open, and the gold chain on his chest rose and fell with each breath.

key: “There is another cellar,” he said. “It has b
prev: He bent, quite slowly, and picked up the cheese.
text: “There is another cellar,” he said. “It has been there for forty years. It is under my own kitchen. It is cold, and dry, and it holds a hundred cheeses, and I have never once thought to look in it, because I had my eye on something grander.” He turned to the four men. “Take the stones home. Pull up the stake. This cave,” and his voice shook, “is the property of the bats.”

key: “Mr. Mayor,” said a small, clear voice.
prev: It was Hopsi. She had stood up. She stood very straight, with her hands folded, in front of the whole village.
text: “I would like to say something,” she said. “It is true. I have only said true things, my whole life, and I have never once said that I was proud of a person. It seems to me that it would be the wrong thing to say, because I could not be sure. But I am sure now.” She looked at Scally, and then at Wen, and at Hal, and at the whole row of faces, one at a time. “I am proud of every one of you. I think so, and I know so. That is all.”

key: Hal sat at the kitchen table with his slate i
prev: That night, the little house by the mill was very quiet.
text: Hal sat at the kitchen table with his slate in front of him, though he was not writing on it. The fire had burned low. His father had gone to bed, with a mug of tea, and a look of great peace, and the cane propped against the wall. The kettle was singing gently on the stove. On the table, at his mother’s elbow, was a plate of pickled onions.

key: “I did not know,” said Hal. “But I wrote it d
prev: “You know?”
text: “I did not know,” said Hal. “But I wrote it down, and I think I had worked it out.” He looked at his slate. “It was the pickled onions. And the knitting. And the way Dr. Liang looked. And you said ‘Oh.’” He took a very long breath. “It is a baby. It is going to be a baby. Like Biscuit, only mine.”

key: “No,” said Hal. “Wait.” He stood up. He went
prev: His mother laughed, quite helplessly, with tears running down her face.
text: “No,” said Hal. “Wait.” He stood up. He went round the table, and put his arms round her, and his face in her shoulder, which smelled of onions and bread and wool. “It is better than acceptable.”

key: Someone was walking along the road toward the
prev: Out in the yard, in the soft April dark, a strange sound drifted along the lane, from the direction of the village. It was a loud, cheerful, tuneless whistle, and under it, steady and unhurried, the creak of boots.
text: Someone was walking along the road toward the mill in the starlight, a very long way off. It was a girl, a stranger, very tall for her age, with hair the color of a struck match, and a long wooden ladder over one shoulder, which she was carrying as easily as another person carries an umbrella. She stopped at the old stone gate. She looked up at the hill, and at the last few bats wheeling black against the stars, and at the little yellow window where a mother and a boy stood together in the lamplight.
